danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 18
paragraphs: Fyrst Bagration, der havde nået det højeste punkt af vores højre fløj, begyndte at ride ned ad bakken mod det sted, hvor geværildens rullen lød, men hvor man på grund af røgen intet kunne se. Jo nærmere de kom hulningen, desto mindre kunne de se, men desto mere mærkede de nærheden af den virkelige slagmark. De begyndte at møde sårede. Én med blødende hoved og uden hue blev slæbt af sted af to soldater, der støttede ham under armene. Der var en gurglende lyd fra hans hals, og han spyttede blod. En kugle havde åbenbart ramt ham i halsen eller munden. En anden gik fast på egne ben, men uden sit gevær, og stønnede højt, mens han svingede armen, der lige var blevet ramt — blodet strømmede fra den ned over hans kappe som fra en flaske. Han var netop blevet såret, og hans ansigt viste snarere frygt end smerte. Da de krydsede en vej, gik de ned ad en stejl skråning og så flere mænd ligge på jorden; de mødte også en flok soldater, hvoraf nogle var usårede. Soldaterne gik op ad bakken tungt åndende og talte trods generalens tilstedeværelse højt og gestikulerede. Foran dem var rækker af grå kapper allerede synlige gennem røgen, og en officer, der fik øje på Bagration, løb råbende efter flokken af flygtende soldater og beordrede dem tilbage. Bagration red op til rækkerne, langs hvilke skud knaldede snart her, snart dér, og overdøvede lyden af stemmer og kommandoråb. Hele luften stank af røg. Soldaternes ophidsede ansigter var sorte af den. Nogle brugte deres ladestokke, andre lagde krudt på fænghullerne eller tog patroner op af tasken, mens atter andre fyrede — skønt det, de fyrede på, ikke kunne ses for røgen, som ingen vind bar bort. En behagelig summen og hvislen af kugler hørtes jævnligt. »Hvad er det her?« tænkte fyrst Andrej, da han nærmede sig flokken af soldater. »Det kan ikke være et angreb, for de rykker ikke frem; det kan ikke være en karré — for de er ikke formeret dertil.«

Regimentskommandøren, en tynd, svagelig gammel mand med et venligt smil — hans øjenlåg dækkede mere end halvdelen af hans gamle øjne, hvilket gav ham et mildt udtryk — red op til Bagration og bød ham velkommen som en vært, der modtager en hædret gæst. Han rapporterede, at hans regiment var blevet angrebet af fransk kavaleri, og at angrebet var slået tilbage, men at han havde mistet mere end halvdelen af sine folk. Han sagde, at angrebet var blevet slået tilbage, idet han brugte dette militære udtryk til at beskrive, hvad der var sket med hans regiment, men i virkeligheden vidste han ikke selv, hvad der var sket i den halve time med de tropper, der var betroet ham, og kunne ikke med sikkerhed sige, om angrebet var slået tilbage, eller hans regiment var brudt op. Alt, hvad han vidste, var, at ved kampens begyndelse begyndte kugler og granater at flyve over hele hans regiment og ramme folk, og at nogen derefter havde råbt: »Kavaleri!« og hans folk var begyndt at skyde. De skød stadig, ikke på kavaleriet, der var forsvundet, men på fransk infanteri, der var kommet ind i hulningen og beskød dem. Fyrst Bagration bøjede hovedet som tegn på, at dette var nøjagtigt, hvad han havde ønsket og forventet. Han vendte sig til sin adjutant og beordrede ham til at hente de to bataljoner af det sjette jægerregiment, som de netop var redet forbi. Fyrst Andrej blev slået af det forandrede udtryk i fyrst Bagrations ansigt i dette øjeblik. Det udtrykte den samlede og lykkelige beslutsomhed, man ser i ansigtet på en mand, der en varm dag tager det sidste tilløb, før han kaster sig i vandet. De matte, søvnige øjne var der ikke længere, ej heller den fornemme attitude af dyb eftertanke. De runde, faste høgeøjne stirrede ivrigt og en smule overlegent frem uden at hvile på noget, skønt hans bevægelser stadig var langsomme og afmålte.

Regimentskommandøren bønfaldt fyrst Bagration om at gå tilbage, da det var for farligt at forblive, hvor de var. »Jeg beder Dem, Deres excellence, for Guds skyld!« blev han ved med at sige, idet han søgte støtte hos en stabsofficer, der vendte sig bort fra ham. »Se dog!« og han henledte opmærksomheden på kuglerne, der uafbrudt hvinede, sang og hvislede omkring dem. Han talte i den bønfaldende og bebrejdende tone, som en tømrer bruger over for en herre, der har grebet en økse: »Vi er vant til det, men De, hr., vil få vabler på hænderne.« Han talte, som om kuglerne ikke kunne dræbe ham, og hans halvlukkede øjne gav hans ord endnu mere overbevisningskraft. Stabsofficeren sluttede sig til oberstens appeller, men Bagration svarede ikke; han gav blot ordre til at standse ilden og formere sig, for at give plads til de to bataljoner, der nærmede sig. Mens han talte, begyndte det røgtæppe, der havde skjult hulningen, drevet af en stigende vind, at bevæge sig fra højre mod venstre, som trukket af en usynlig hånd, og bakken overfor med franskmændene i bevægelse åbenbarede sig for dem. Alle blikke hæftede sig uvilkårligt på denne franske kolonne, der rykkede frem mod dem og snoede sig ned over det ujævne terræn. Man kunne allerede skelne soldaternes lodne huer, kende officererne fra de menige og se fanen blafrende på sin stang.
»De marcherer pragtfuldt,« bemærkede nogen i Bagrations følge.
Kolonnehoveden var allerede steget ned i hulningen. Sammenstødet ville finde sted på denne side af den...

Resterne af regimentet, der havde været i kamp, formerede sig hurtigt og rykkede til højre; bagfra kom to bataljoner af det sjette jægerregiment i fin orden, idet de spredte efternølerne. Før de havde nået Bagration, kunne man høre den tunge, taktfaste trampen af massen af marcherende mænd. På deres venstre fløj, nærmest Bagration, marcherede en kompagnichef, en flot, rund mand med et fjollet og lykkeligt udtryk — den samme mand, der var stormet ud af flethytten. I det øjeblik tænkte han tydeligvis på intet andet end, hvor flot han ville tage sig ud, idet han passerede kommandøren.

Med selvtilfredsheden hos en mand på parade trådte han let med sine muskuløse ben, som svævede han, og strakte sig til sin fulde højde uden den mindste anstrengelse — hans lethed stod i kontrast til soldaternes tunge trampen, som holdt trit med ham. Tæt op ad benet bar han en smal, udtrukken sabel (lille, krum og ikke som et rigtigt våben) og så nu på de overordnede officerer, nu tilbage på sine folk uden at miste takten, mens hele hans kraftige krop drejede smidigt. Det var, som om alle hans sjælekræfter var samlet om at passere kommandøren på bedste vis, og da han følte, at det gik godt, var han lykkelig. »Venstre... venstre... venstre...« syntes han at gentage for sig selv ved hvert andet skridt; og i takt med dette, med strenge men varierede ansigter, marcherede muren af soldater, tyngede af randsler og geværer, i trit, og hver eneste af disse hundreder af soldater syntes at gentage for sig selv ved hvert andet skridt: »Venstre... venstre... venstre...« En svær major snoede sig om en busk, pustende og ude af trit; en soldat, der var sakket bagud, med frygt i ansigtet over sin forseelse, løb i trav, pustende, for at indhente sit kompagni. En kanonkugle, der kløvede luften, fløj over hovederne på Bagration og hans følge og slog ned i kolonnen i takt med »venstre... venstre!« »Slut op!« lød kompagnichefens stemme i kæk tone. Soldaterne gik i en halvkreds udenom det sted, hvor kuglen var faldet, og en gammel tropper på fløjen, en underofficer, der havde standset ved de faldne, løb for at nå sin plads og faldt med et hop ind i takten — han så vredt tilbage, og gennem den ildevarslende stilhed og det regelmæssige tramp af fødder, der ensformigt slog mod jorden, syntes man at høre: venstre... venstre... venstre.
»Godt gået, gutter!« sagde fyrst Bagration.

»Glad for at gøre vores bedste, Deres exc'lence!« lød et forvirret råb fra rækkerne. En gnaven soldat, der marcherede på venstre fløj, vendte øjnene mod Bagration, mens han råbte, med et udtryk der syntes at sige: »Det ved vi godt selv!« En anden, uden at se sig om, som om han frygtede at slappe af, råbte med vidåben mund og passerede videre.
Ordren lød om at gøre holdt og aflægge ranslerne.

Bagration red langs de rækker, der var marcheret forbi ham, og steg af. Han gav tøjlerne til en kosaksoldat, tog sin filtkappe af og rakte den fra sig, strakte sine ben og rettede på huen. Den franske kolonnes hoved med officererne i spidsen viste sig nedenfra bakken.

»Fremad, med Gud!« sagde Bagration med en fast, klangfuld stemme, vendte sig et øjeblik mod frontlinjen, og idet han let svingede armene, gik han fremad med den lidt usikre gang, en kavalerist har, over den ujævne mark. Fyrst Andrej følte, at en usynlig kraft drev ham fremad, og oplevede en stor lykkefølelse.

Franskmændene var allerede tæt på. Fyrst Andrej, der gik ved siden af Bagration, kunne tydeligt skelne deres bandolierer, røde epauletter og endda deres ansigter. (Han så tydeligt en gammel fransk officer, der med gamascher og udadvendte tæer med besvær klatrede op ad bakken.) Fyrst Bagration gav ingen yderligere ordrer og fortsatte tavst sin gang foran rækkerne. Pludselig faldt skud efter skud fra franskmændene, røg viste sig langs hele deres uregelmæssige rækker, og geværskud gjaldede. Flere af vores folk faldt, blandt dem den rundkindede officer, der så muntert og selvtilfreds havde marcheret. Men i det øjeblik det første skud lød, vendte Bagration sig om og råbte: »Hurra!«
»Hurra—a—a—a!« lød et langtrukket råb fra vores rækker, og forbi Bagration, idet de kapløb med hinanden, stormede de i en uregelmæssig, men glad og ivrig flok ned ad bakken mod den uordnede fjende.

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: Having reached the highest point of the right flank, Prince Bagration began riding downhill toward the sound of gunfire, though the smoke made it impossible to see anything. The closer they got to the hollow, the less they could see but the more intensely they felt the proximity of the actual fighting. They started meeting wounded men. One, his head bleeding and his cap gone, was being dragged along by two soldiers gripping him under the arms. He was gurgling and spitting blood—a bullet had clearly struck him in the mouth or throat. Another walked along steadily under his own power, but without his musket, groaning loudly and swinging his arm, which had just been wounded. Blood streamed from it down over his greatcoat as from an uncorked bottle. He'd only just been hit, and his face showed more fear than pain. Crossing a road, they descended a steep slope and saw several men lying on the ground; they also encountered a crowd of soldiers, some unwounded. The soldiers were climbing the hill, breathing hard, and despite the general's presence, they were talking loudly and waving their arms. Up ahead, through the smoke, rows of gray cloaks were already visible, and an officer who spotted Bagration ran shouting after the retreating soldiers, trying to order them back. Bagration rode up to the line, along which gunfire crackled first here, then there, drowning out voices and shouted commands. The air was thick with smoke. The soldiers' excited faces were blackened with it. Some were ramming charges, others pouring powder into touchpans or pulling cartridges from their pouches, still others were firing—though through the drifting, windless smoke, who they were firing at was impossible to tell. A pleasant humming and whistling of bullets filled the air. "What's going on here?" thought Prince Andrew as he approached the crowd. "It can't be an attack—they aren't moving. It can't be a square—they aren't formed up for that."

The regimental commander, a thin, frail-looking old man with a kind smile—his drooping eyelids covering more than half his eyes and giving him a gentle expression—rode up to Bagration and greeted him like a host welcoming an honored guest. He reported that his regiment had been attacked by French cavalry, and that although the attack had been repulsed, he'd lost more than half his men. He used the military term "repulsed" to describe what had happened, but in truth he himself had no idea what had actually occurred during that half hour. All he really knew was that at the start of the action, shells and bullets had begun flying all over his regiment, hitting his men. Then someone had shouted "Cavalry!" and his soldiers had started shooting. They were still shooting now—not at the cavalry, which had vanished, but at French infantry that had moved into the hollow and was firing at them. Prince Bagration nodded, as though this was precisely what he'd expected. Turning to his adjutant, he ordered him to bring down the two battalions of the Sixth Chasseurs they'd just passed. Prince Andrew was struck by the change in Bagration's expression at that moment. His face now showed the focused, joyful determination you see in a man who, on a sweltering day, takes one final running start before plunging into the water. The dull, sleepy look was gone, and so was the pretense of deep deliberation. His round, steady, hawklike eyes stared ahead with eager, almost disdainful intensity, fixing on nothing in particular, though his movements remained slow and measured.

The regimental commander pleaded with Bagration to go back, insisting it was too dangerous where they stood. "Please, your excellency, for God's sake!" he kept saying, glancing at a staff officer for support—but the staff officer looked away. "There—do you see?" He gestured at the bullets that whistled, sang, and hissed past them constantly. He spoke in the imploring tone a carpenter uses with a gentleman who has picked up an axe: "We're used to this sort of thing, but you, sir, will blister your hands." He spoke as if the bullets couldn't possibly kill him, and his half-shut eyes gave his words even more persuasive force. The staff officer added his pleas to the colonel's, but Bagration didn't respond. He simply ordered the troops to stop firing and re-form to make room for the two approaching battalions. As he spoke, the curtain of smoke hiding the hollow was swept from right to left by a rising breeze, as if pulled by an invisible hand, and the opposite hill—with French soldiers moving about on it—was suddenly revealed. Every eye locked instinctively on the French column advancing toward them, winding down over the broken ground. You could already make out the soldiers' shaggy caps, tell the officers from the enlisted men, and see the regimental standard flapping against its staff.
"They march beautifully," someone in Bagration's group remarked.
The head of the French column had already descended into the hollow. The collision would happen on this side of it...

The remnants of the regiment that had been engaged quickly reformed and shifted to the right. From behind them, sweeping aside the stragglers, came two battalions of the Sixth Chasseurs in excellent order. Before they'd even reached Bagration, the heavy, rhythmic tread of massed men marching in step could be heard. On their left flank, nearest to Bagration, marched a company commander—a round-faced, handsome man with a stupid, blissful expression: the same officer who had rushed out of the wattle hut earlier. At that moment, he was clearly thinking about nothing except how magnificent he would look as he passed the commander.

With the self-assurance of a man on parade, he stepped lightly on his muscular legs as if gliding, stretching to his full height effortlessly, his ease a stark contrast to the heavy tramp of the soldiers keeping pace beside him. He carried a narrow, unsheathed sword close against his leg—small, curved, not really a weapon at all—and kept glancing now at the senior officers, now back at his men, all without breaking stride, his whole powerful body pivoting fluidly. It was as if every fiber of his being were focused on looking perfect as he passed the commander, and since he felt he was succeeding, he was perfectly happy. "Left... left... left..." he seemed to repeat to himself with each step, and in time to this rhythm, with stern but varied expressions, the wall of soldiers burdened with packs and muskets marched forward, each one seeming to repeat that same silent cadence: "Left... left... left..." A portly major skirted a bush, puffing and losing the beat. A soldier who'd fallen behind, alarm on his face at his own transgression, trotted to catch up. A cannonball sliced through the air over the heads of Bagration and his suite and slammed into the column, right in the rhythm of "Left... left!" "Close up!" rang out the company commander's voice, jaunty as ever. The soldiers curved around the spot where the ball had struck, and an old noncommissioned officer on the flank, who had stopped beside the fallen men, ran to catch up with his line. With a little hop he fell back into step, glanced back angrily, and through the ominous silence, beneath the regular tramp of boots striking the ground in unison, you could almost hear it still: left... left... left...
"Well done, lads!" said Prince Bagration.

"Glad to serve, your ex-len-cy!" came back a ragged shout from the ranks. One grim-faced soldier on the left flank turned his eyes toward Bagration as he shouted, his expression seeming to say: "We know that ourselves!" Another, not daring to look around for fear of losing focus, shouted with his mouth stretched wide and marched on.
The order came to halt and drop packs.

Bagration rode along the ranks that had just marched past and dismounted. He handed his reins to a Cossack, took off his felt cloak and passed it over, stretched his legs, and straightened his cap. The head of the French column, officers in the lead, appeared from below the hill.

"Forward, with God!" said Bagration in a resolute, ringing voice. He turned briefly to face the front line and, swinging his arms slightly, began walking forward over the rough ground with the awkward, rolling gait of a cavalryman. Prince Andrew felt an invisible force drawing him forward, and a surge of happiness swept through him.

The French were already close. Walking beside Bagration, Prince Andrew could clearly make out their bandoliers, red epaulets, even their faces. He distinctly saw an old French officer with gaitered legs and feet turned out, struggling up the hill. Prince Bagration gave no more orders and walked silently on ahead of the ranks. Then, all at once, a volley of shots erupted from the French side—smoke appeared along their ragged line—and musket fire crackled. Several Russian soldiers fell, among them the round-faced officer who had marched so cheerfully, so proudly. But at the very instant the first shot rang out, Bagration looked back and shouted, "Hurrah!"

"Hurrah-ah-ah!" A long, drawn-out roar rose from the Russian ranks, and the men surged past Bagration—racing each other, an irregular but joyful, eager crowd—charging down the hill toward the disordered enemy.
